title: Verifier‑Augmented vs. LLM‑Only NetOps Agents: A Paired Evaluation on an Action‑Aware Staging Benchmark
abstract: We present a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark (ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1). The preregistration (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) fixed N=400 paired tasks, gpt-5-mini as the generator, and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer, with shared_initial_generation semantics (one shared LLM candidate per task delivered to both conditions). Key confirmatory outcomes (archived artifacts): complete_pairs = 400; baseline_success_count = 400/400; guarded_success_count = 400/400; paired contingency n_11 = 400, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0; observed paired difference = 0.0; preregistered permutation p = 1.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples); Cohen's h = 0.0. Importantly, the preregistered combination of shared_initial_generation semantics and reuse of the same deterministic validator as runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer produced a deterministic ceiling effect (universal acceptance) that rendered the primary estimand uninformative for assessing generator×guard closed‑loop dynamics in this run. We archive all execution and analysis artifacts and present an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of why the design produced a null outcome, representative task difficulty diagnostics, and concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations for hardening future benchmarks so they expose generator×guard interactions.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent into network configuration artifacts and staged rollout procedures (canaries, progressive delivery, rollback). Prior work shows LLMs can generate syntactically plausible configurations but flags operational risks—hallucination, misordered actions, and poor handling of staged semantics—that threaten availability and safety when changes are applied. Verifier‑augmented generate–validate–repair pipelines and deterministic network verifiers are natural mitigations, but open questions remain about whether and when runtime verifiers measurably improve end‑to‑end safety for agentic NetOps workflows. To probe this, we preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark (ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1) that simulates intent→configuration tasks with staged rollout semantics. Research question. Under ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1, does integrating a deterministic runtime validator with an LLM generator increase the paired safe‑deploy rate relative to an LLM‑only pipeline? The primary estimand was the paired difference in safe‑deploy rate (guarded − baseline) in a confirmatory paired design with N=400 tasks. Contribution. We (1) provide a preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5; (2) show, based on archived traces and reconciled accounting, that shared_initial_generation semantics combined with reuse of a single deterministic validator produced a deterministic ceiling effect and a null primary outcome; and (3) give artifact‑grounded benchmark‑hardening recommendations to preserve statistical signal in future confirmatory evaluations.
sections.related_work: LLM‑based intent→configuration and IaC automation work establishes that language models can synthesize usable configuration templates in controlled settings (intent‑based translation, PreConfig, GraphSynth). Verifier‑guided loops in Infrastructure‑as‑Code (e.g., TerraFormer) and generate–validate–repair architectures demonstrate correctness gains in provisioning contexts and motivate closed‑loop verifier integration for NetOps. Deterministic network verification and reachability tools (header‑space and related approaches) effectively detect configuration errors in emulated/offline settings, though tool scope and modelling assumptions vary. Agentic and tool‑augmented LLM architectures (ReAct, RAG, multi‑agent orchestrations) enhance functionality for AIOps and RCA but introduce new failure modes (hallucination, misapplied tools, miscalibrated confidence) that motivate runtime guardrails and staged deployment. Surveyed literature identifies an evaluation gap: few community benchmarks evaluate action‑taking agents end‑to‑end with staged rollout, rollback, provenance, and runtime blocking. Our experiment operationalizes a compact action‑aware staging benchmark under a strict preregistered design to directly probe runtime verifier utility under those constraints.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The study preregistration (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) fixed a paired binary confirmatory design with N=400 tasks and the primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The analysis executor paired_binary_analysis_v1 implements the preregistered permutation‑based paired difference test (two‑sided, α=0.05) and an exact McNemar two‑sided test as corroboration; bootstrap percentile CIs (seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) were frozen for secondary summaries.

Adapter semantics and shared generation (critical design choice). Execution used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family with declared generator gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer. A preregistered, deliberate adapter setting—shared_initial_generation = true (independent_condition_generation = false)—requested a single deterministic LLM generation per task and delivered that identical candidate to both baseline and guarded episodes. The intent of this isolation was to measure validator acceptance on identical generator outputs; however, combined with a deterministic validator, this choice removes inter‑condition generator variance and can create ceiling scenarios.

Model‑call accounting and replay checks. The preregistered mapping of episodes to model calls produced planned episodes = 800 (two episodes per task) while model_calls_used = 400 because of shared generation (one LLM call per task). The preregistration required deterministic three‑replay consistency checks: each agent+simulator pair is replayed three times and any non‑identical replay outcomes or simulator errors would be flagged and excluded from the primary analysis. The missingness plan mandated automated exclusion without human adjudication. Deterministic replay checks passed for all pairs in this execution.

Episode flow, validator policy, and repair rules. For each task the adapter: (a) requested a shared initial candidate from gpt‑5‑mini; (b) delivered it to both baseline and guarded episodes; (c) for guarded episodes deterministic_netops_validator_v5 applied full intent‑constraint validation and could invoke up to one repair attempt per the preregistered repair policy. Validator_trace entries capture repair_applied, normalized_configuration, validation_before/after states, difficulty metadata, and final validity decisions. In the executed run repair_applied = false for all episodes.

Task generation and difficulty metadata. Tasks were generated deterministically with deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and include structured per‑task difficulty labels (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, pattern, required_command_count, level ∈ {medium, hard, very_hard}). Representative examples (first six tasks) show a mix of medium, hard, and very_hard patterns; the full per‑task labels for N=400 are archived in the execution bundle (execution/task_manifest.jsonl) for auditor aggregation. Aggregated counts by difficulty are available in that manifest; we report representative sample counts here as illustration while the full per‑task labels remain archived for reproducibility.

Analysis plan and inferential precautions. Primary confirmatory analysis uses the preregistered permutation‑based paired difference test and reports exact permutation p‑values and Cohen's h for proportions. The primary analysis excludes tasks flagged by deterministic replay as nondeterministic. Sensitivity analyses specified in the preregistration (treating excluded pairs as failures, restricted permutations) are implemented and archived but were not required because no exclusions occurred. Secondary analyses (bootstrap CIs for median time‑to‑rollback, repair‑attempt accounting) were preregistered as descriptive outcomes.

sections.discussion:
Diagnosis of the null primary outcome. Two preregistered design choices combined to create the observed deterministic ceiling: (1) shared_initial_generation delivered identical generator outputs to both baseline and guarded episodes, intentionally isolating validator acceptance on identical strings; and (2) the runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer were the same deterministic implementation (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). When a deterministic validator consistently accepts the shared candidate, both conditions necessarily produce identical safe‑deploy outcomes and the primary estimand becomes uninformative for generator×guard closed‑loop dynamics.

Consequences for power and interpretation. The preregistered power rationale assumed non‑ceiling baseline rates and intra‑pair variability (target detectable absolute increase ≈10 percentage points with N=400). The observed ceiling invalidates these assumptions and collapses inferential uncertainty: correct statistical tests (permutation and McNemar) reflect identical outcomes (p = 1.0) but cannot adjudicate whether independent generator variance would have produced guardable failures. Thus the null result should not be interpreted as evidence that runtime verification is unnecessary generally; instead it is a direct artifact of frozen design choices and implementation homogeneity.

Artifact‑grounded recommendations for benchmark hardening. Based on the archived validator_trace structure, execution accounting, and reconciled model call mapping, we recommend the following implementable steps for future preregistered runs that aim to preserve signal for guard interventions: (A) set independent_condition_generation = true (independent per‑condition generator samples) so each condition receives independent outputs and generator variance can expose guard interventions; (B) separate runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer implementations (or use independent adjudicators) to avoid conflating acceptance and scoring; (C) preregister a controlled fraction of adversarial/perturbation seeds to guarantee measurable baseline failure rates and preserve power; (D) stratify sampling to oversample very_hard patterns or include difficulty‑stratified quotas so the benchmark contains non‑negligible error rates; (E) enable and instrument repair attempts and rollback timing as preregistered secondary outcomes to measure mitigation efficacy. Each recommendation is anchored in artifacts: validator_trace fields (repair_applied, validation_before/after, difficulty metadata), model_call accounting, and task_manifest difficulty labels.

Threats to validity and generalizability. Internal validity: the shared_generation design and reuse of the same deterministic validator for runtime and scoring conflate acceptance and measurement. Construct validity: deterministic validator decisions may not reflect production noisy telemetry or operator ambiguity. External validity: single generator (gpt‑5‑mini) and single validator limit generalization across models, validator types, and real networks. Conclusion validity: the ceiling removes variance needed for hypothesis testing and invalidates the preregistered power calculation for the primary estimand.

Operational implications. For practitioners evaluating verifier integration, two practical lessons emerge from the archived traces: (1) design choices that remove generation variance can mask the effectivity of runtime guards; (2) independent adjudication channels (distinct scorers or human review) are important for measuring guard impact. Benchmarks intended to validate runtime safety mechanisms should preserve both generator variance and independent adjudication to maintain statistical signal.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark. Under the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and a deterministic validator used for both runtime guarding and post‑hoc scoring, all shared candidates satisfied the validator and both conditions achieved 100% safe‑deploy across N=400 pairs (paired difference = 0.0; permutation p = 1.0). This deterministic ceiling effect stems from preregistered design and implementation homogeneity and renders the primary estimand uninformative for generator×guard closed‑loop interactions in this run. We archive the preregistration and full execution/analysis artifacts to support reproducibility and to enable hardened follow‑on experiments (independent generation, adversarial seeding, heterogeneous validators) that exercise blocking, repair, and rollback behaviors. Our artifact‑grounded hardening recommendations provide concrete steps researchers can preregister to preserve statistical signal when evaluating runtime verifier utility in NetOps settings.

limitations: Benchmark hardness and ceiling effect: under preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 so the guard had no opportunity to alter outcomes; this makes the primary estimand effectively untestable in this run and invalidates the original power rationale.

Model and scope: the experiment used a single generator (gpt-5-mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); results do not generalize across models, validators, or production heterogeneity.

Construct validity: the same deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementation served as both runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer; this conflation produces concordant acceptance/scoring and limits inference about independent closed‑loop verifier utility.

Shared candidate semantics: preregistered shared_initial_generation (one LLM generation per task shared by both conditions) intentionally reduces generation variance and therefore limits inference to the validator’s behavior on identical candidates rather than full generator+guard closed‑loop interactions.

Synthetic environment and external validity: the simulator and validator do not fully model production telemetry noise, operator workflows, or adversarial actor behaviours; external validity to live networks is limited.

Adversarial robustness untested: adversarial or distribution‑shifted prompts and generator faults that could trigger guard interventions were not exercised in this run and remain open for future work.

Aggregated difficulty reporting gap: the full per‑task difficulty labels for all N=400 are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and can be aggregated by auditors; the manuscript reports representative sample counts (first six tasks) to illustrate benchmark diversity but does not fabricate the aggregated N=400 counts.
